system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 59-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and HIV presented with a partially dislodged right femoral tunneled dialysis catheter, preventing scheduled dialysis. She also reported nontraumatic pain in her left first and second toes. The catheter was successfully exchanged over a wire in the interventional radiology suite without complications. Hemodialysis was completed the following day using the new catheter. Foot X-ray showed no fracture, and the toe pain was managed symptomatically. The patient initially refused her home HIV medications but was counseled on adherence and agreed to resume treatment. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor the catheter site and maintain medication compliance.
problems: Mechanical complication of other vascular device, implant, and graft
Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status

INDICATION:  ___ female with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. 
Right tunneled hemodialysis line discontinued for infection.  New left
tunneled femoral line and venogram requested based on worsening lower
extremity edema.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (resident), Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr.
___ (attending, present and supervising throughout).

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
fentanyl (250 mcg) and Versed (4 mg) over a total intraservice time of 1 hour
and 15 minutes, during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
monitored continuously by an independent radiology nurse.  1% lidocaine and
lidocaine with epinephrine were administered to the skin and subcutaneous
tissues for local anesthesia.

RADIATION:  85 mGy, 17 minutes.

CONTRAST:  60 mL Optiray.

PROCEDURES:

1.  Left common femoral venous access under ultrasound guidance.

2.  Left common iliac and IVC venography.

3.  Placement of a tunneled HD catheter via the left femoral vein.

PROCEDURE DETAIL:  After discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to
the procedure, written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought
to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The left
groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A preprocedure
timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ protocol.

Using a combination of fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, the left common
femoral vein was accessed with a 19-gauge needle.  A ___ wire was then
advanced through the needle into the lower IVC.  A small skin ___ was made
over the needle which was then removed.  A 5 ___ sheath was then advanced
over the wire into the left common iliac vein.  Subsequently, a venogram was
performed with findings described below.  Next, a 0.035 Glidewire was advanced
through the sheath and multiple attempts were made with the assistance of both
an Omniflush catheter and a C2 Cobra Glide catheter to cannulate the right
common iliac vein, but a decision was made to turn our attention back to
placement of the tunneled line due to patient discomfort.  

The Glidewire was advanced into the right atrium and the appropriate
measurements were taken.  After additional local anesthesia, a 1 cm skin
incision was made on the left upper thigh approximately 8 cm from the
venotomy.  A 15.5 ___ tunneled catheter was passed from the incision to the
venotomy site with the aid of a metal tunneling device.  The venotomy tract
was then dilated with 12- and ___ dilators.  A peel-away sheath was
passed over the wire.  The wire and inner cannula were removed and the
catheter was passed through the peel-away sheath.  The peel-away sheath was
then removed while the catheter was pushed into the right atrium.  This was
confirmed by fluoroscopy demonstrating the catheter tip in the right atrium. 
Both lumens aspirated blood and flushed easily.  The catheter was secured with
two 0 silk sutures.  The venotomy site was closed with a ___ Vicryl
subcuticular stitch.  Dry sterile dressings were applied.  There was no
immediate complication.

FINDINGS: Flow obstruction in the IVC / confluence of the iliac veins with
multiple collaterals.  Filling of the right common iliac via collaterals. 
Filling defect at the the right common iliac vein just proximal to the
confluence consistent with either clot or stenosis. Inability to cross this
area of stenosis with a guidewire coming over the iliac confluence, consistent
with stenosis. A more detailed venogram could not be completed due to the
patient's discomfort, and will require general anesthesia on a future visit. 

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated left common iliac and IVC venograms and placement
of a tunneled hemodialysis catheter via the left common femoral vein.  The tip
is located in the right atrium and the catheter is ready for use.

To clarify, the tip of the left common femoral vein dialysis catheter was
positioned in the mid right atrium under real time fluoroscopic guidance.

INDICATION:  ___ female with end-stage renal disease on dialysis with
complicated access history and concern for IVC stenosis on prior tunneled line
placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PHYSICIANS: Dr. ___ (fellow) and Dr. ___ (attending, present
and supervising throughout).

ANESTHESIA/MEDICATIONS:  General anesthesia was induced. Heparin was
administered prior to balloon plasty, 3000 units.  

RADIATION:  599 mGy, 34 minutes 9 seconds.

CONTRAST:  230 cc IV Optiray.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Right and left common femoral vein access.
2.  Bilateral common iliac venography and IVC venography.
3.  Balloon plasty via bilateral accesses in the IVC up to 14 mm.
4.  Post-balloon plasty venograms.
5.  Replacement of the existing left femoral tunneled catheter with a new 55cm
15.5F tunneled hemodialysis catheter.

PROCEDURE DETAIL: After discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to
the procedure, written informed consent was obtained.  The patient was brought
to the Angiography Suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ protocol.  The
bilateral groins and the indwelling left tunneled catheter were prepped and
draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Under ultrasound guidance, the patent and compressible right common femoral
vein was accessed using a micropuncture needle.  An 0.018 nitinol wire was
advanced into the common iliac vein under fluoroscopic guidance.  A small skin
incision was made and the needle was removed and exchanged for a micropuncture
sheath.  The inner portion of the sheath and the wire were removed and a
___ wire was advanced through the micropuncture sheath.A ___ vascular
sheath was then placed.  

Next, the left tunneled groin line was aspirated and flushed.  An Amplatz wire
was then advanced through one of the lumens and the tunneled catheter was
easily removed.  A 12 ___ sheath was advanced through the tunnel into the
common iliac vein with good hemostasis.  Next, an Omniflush catheter was
advanced over the wire into the lower IVC and a venogram was performed
demonstrating a 2cm segment of marked (85-90%) caval stenosis at the level of
the suprarenal IVC with extensive right perinephric and perlilumbar
collaterals. The Omniflush catheter was advanced further into the IVC and a
second venogram was performed demonstrating brisk flow above the level of the
renal veins.  

Next, we turned our attention to the right groin access.    A venogram was
performed demonstrating multiple pelvic collaterals arising from the right
common iliac vein and again a caval stenosis was again noted.  At this time, a
decision was made to perform angioplasty of the IVC. Systemic heparin was
administered. Sequential venoplasty was performed via the left femoral access
with 8mm 10 mm, 12 mm and 14 mm balloons.  There was a slight persistent waist
in the mid IVC with a 14-mm balloon however further inflation was not
possible.  Subsequently, a venogram was repeated on the right and demonstrated
preferential flow from the right common iliac through a collateral that then
joined the right renal vein and reconstituted through a collateral to the IVC.
A decision was made to repeat balloon plasty via the right common femoral
access through the entire IVC and proximal aspect of the common iliac vein
with a 12-mm balloon.  

A final cavogram demonstrated improvef flow through the IVC following plasty

Finally, we removed the sheath on the left and placed a 16 ___ peel-away
sheath through which a new hemodialysis catheter was threaded over the wire
into the IVC.  The peel-away sheath was removed and the catheter was advanced
over the wire until the tip was positioned in the right atrium.  The wire was
removed.  Both lumens aspirated and flushed easily.
A cavogram performed with the dialysis catheter in situ however showed partial
occlussion of the stenotic IVC by the 15.5F dialysis catheter.  The catheter
was secured to the skin with ___ silk sutures.  A dry sterile dressing was
applied.  The right femoral sheath was removed and manual compression was held
for 10 minutes for optimal hemostasis.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complication and
was transported immediately to the PACU.

FINDINGS:

1.  Marked caval stenosis up to approximately 90%, with a linear channel in
the IVC suggestive of a pericatheter fibrin sheath.

2.  Balloon plasty of the IVC to 14 mm with improved flow but slight residual
waste at the level just above the renal veins.
    Despite considearble improvement following balloon plasty , the presence
of a partially occlussive dialysis catheter across the stenosis means there
remains a significant  flow impedement across the IVC

3.  15.5 ___ hemodialysis catheter via the left common femoral approach.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Bilateral common iliac and IVC venography demonstrating a tight (90%)
caval stenosis and extensive right perinephric and pelvic collateralization. 
Uncomplicated IVC balloon plasty to 14mm with good angiogaphic result prior to
replacement of the dialysis catheter. Cavogram with the catheter in situ
however shows persistent , short, flow limiting stenosis at the level of
suprarenal IVC. 

2.  Replacement of the existing 15.5 ___ tunneled hemodialysis catheter in
the left common femoral vein with a new 15.5 ___ catheter via the existing
tract.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today with chills and pain at your dialysis line site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling feverish all day. My right groin line is really sore and there’s some yellow drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you had dialysis earlier but they had to slow it down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it hurt when they started. They gave me vancomycin and sent blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right step. We’re concerned your catheter might be infected. We’ll check your labs and do a CT scan to make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having more vaginal discharge and burning. And it feels like I need to pee, but I don’t make urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. We’ll examine that and take some swabs to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this all related to my dialysis line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fever and pain likely are. The abdominal discomfort might be referred from the groin. We’ll keep investigating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan came back clear—no abscess or other issues in your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. Your white count is low, which is concerning. We’re starting antibiotics and will likely need to remove the infected catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Remove it? Where will I get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a new one, probably in your left groin. You’ve had trouble with fistulas before, so a new tunneled line is safest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to remove your right catheter today. The ultrasound shows your left vein is open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local numbing and some sedation. You’ll feel pressure but not sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The old catheter is out. We sent the tip for culture. You’re on cefepime for now, but we’ll adjust based on results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any word on the vaginal discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Swabs were negative for yeast, BV, and STIs. We’re treating it as possible irritation. We’ll follow up with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are negative so far, which is good. But the catheter tip grew MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA? Isn’t that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we caught it early. You’ll need four weeks of IV vancomycin during dialysis to clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? Could it spread there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echo—no sign of infection on your heart valves. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vaginal cultures came back negative. We’ll still follow up with your doctor for a Pap smear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the itching all over? It’s worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your eosinophil count is high. It could be from infection, meds, or allergies. We’re adding hydroxyzine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see an allergist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll refer you after discharge. It might help explain the skin issues and blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re placing a new dialysis line in your left groin. We’ll also do a venogram to check your veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the venogram?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had swelling in your legs. We want to make sure there’s no blockage in your large veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new line is in. The venogram showed a tight narrowing in your IVC. We couldn’t fully treat it today due to discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might contribute to swelling. We’ll plan a procedure under general anesthesia to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your new line is working, and you’re tolerating dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt dizzy during dialysis yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure dropped. We gave fluids. You were on midodrine before—did you stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t fill the prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting it. It helps prevent low BP during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is stable. HIV panel shows very low CD4—27 cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s bad, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it means your immune system is weak. That’s why infections like this can happen. We’re keeping you on your HIV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping them sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but they’re crucial. We’ll go over strategies to help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re doing another procedure to open the blockage in your IVC and replace the dialysis catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? So soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because the narrowing is affecting blood flow. We’ll use balloons to stretch it open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We opened the stenosis and replaced the catheter. There’s still some narrowing with the catheter in place, but it’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. A stent might help long-term, but we’ll discuss that with vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home today. You’ll continue vancomycin with dialysis for four more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP for a Pap smear, dermatology for your skin, and possibly an allergist. Keep taking all your meds, especially HIV and midodrine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given during dialysis. Your dialysis team will handle it. Call if you develop fever, chills, or redness at the catheter site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take everything. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Take care of yourself and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your strongyloides test is pending. If positive, we’ll treat it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your PTH is high—300. Keep taking cinacalcet and follow up with nephrology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping that too sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important for your bones and calcium. Let’s work on a pill organizer to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That might help. I get confused with so many pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll set you up with resources to make it easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by being honest. We’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already. Just glad the infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So do we. Keep up the good work. You’ll get stronger every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember, call if anything changes—fever, pain, swelling, or if you miss a dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Stay on your meds and keep your appointments. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 59-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and HIV presented with chills, fever, and purulent drainage from her right femoral tunneled dialysis catheter, concerning for catheter-related infection. She also reported new vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain. Blood and catheter tip cultures confirmed MRSA infection, prompting removal of the infected catheter and placement of a new left femoral tunneled line. She completed a dose of vancomycin and was transitioned to a four-week course administered during dialysis. An echocardiogram showed no evidence of endocarditis. A venogram revealed significant IVC stenosis, which was partially treated with balloon angioplasty during replacement of the catheter. Her vaginal symptoms were evaluated and found to be non-infectious. She was restarted on midodrine for dialysis-related hypotension and counseled on adherence to her HIV and other chronic medications. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans for outpatient follow-up in dermatology, primary care, and possible allergy and vascular surgery.
problems: Bloodstream infection due to central venous catheter
Other complications due to renal dialysis device, implant, and graft
Herpes zoster with other nervous system complications
